High-protein diet

The complete guide

A high-protein diet is more than just a fitness trend – it's scientifically sound and offers benefits for muscle building, weight management, metabolism, and healthy aging. This guide explains how much protein you really need, which sources are optimal, and how you can check your protein intake.

What does a high-protein diet mean?

A high-protein or protein-prioritized diet describes a nutritional approach in which protein is no longer considered a supplement, but rather a central building block of every meal. While traditional dietary recommendations often focus on carbohydrates and treat protein as secondary, the high-protein philosophy reverses this hierarchy. The basic idea: Plan your protein intake first, then fill it up with vegetables, and supplement with carbohydrates and fats as needed.

The scientific basis for this approach is robust and constantly growing. Protein is the only macronutrient that your body cannot efficiently store – unlike fat or carbohydrates, which can be stored in virtually unlimited quantities as adipose tissue or glycogen. This means that you need to consume sufficient protein daily to ensure the diverse functions of this essential nutrient: muscle maintenance and growth, immune function, hormone production, enzyme activity, and the continuous renewal of cells and tissues.

What exactly constitutes a "high protein" diet varies depending on the source and context. The official recommendations of the German Nutrition Society (DGE) are 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight – a value that is increasingly criticized as a minimum to prevent deficiencies, not as optimal for health and performance. Modern nutritional science and sports medicine recommend significantly higher values: 1.2 to 2.0 grams per kilogram of body weight for the general population, 1.6 to 2.2 grams for athletes and active individuals, and sometimes even more for older adults who want to counteract age-related muscle loss.

In practice, a high-protein diet for someone weighing 75 kilograms means a daily protein intake of approximately 120 to 150 grams – two to three times what many people actually consume. This amount requires conscious planning and often a change in eating habits. Instead of a carbohydrate-rich breakfast of muesli or toast, eggs, quark, or protein-rich smoothies take center stage. Lunch and dinner are built around a substantial protein source – meat, fish, legumes, or tofu – rather than being served as a side dish to pasta or rice.

The shift towards protein prioritization is not just an individual dietary trend, but reflects a growing scientific understanding of how nutrition influences health, body composition, and longevity. Research over the past two decades has shown that higher protein intake—as part of a balanced diet—is associated with a variety of positive health outcomes, from better body composition and more stable blood sugar levels to a reduced risk of age-related diseases.

The Science of Protein – Why Your Body Needs It

Protein is far more than just 'muscle food' – it's the universal building block of your body. To understand why an adequate protein supply is so fundamentally important, it's worth taking a look at the biochemical basis and the diverse functions that proteins perform in your body.

At the molecular level, proteins consist of chains of amino acids – the proverbial building blocks of life. There are 20 different amino acids, which can be combined in various ways and sequences to form hundreds of thousands of different proteins. Nine of these amino acids are considered essential: your body cannot produce them itself and relies on obtaining them through food. These essential amino acids – histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine – must be consumed regularly and in sufficient quantities to maintain all protein-dependent bodily functions.

Structural functions

The most obvious role of protein is structural: your muscles are made up of about 80 percent protein (based on dry mass). But bones, tendons, ligaments, skin, hair, and nails are also protein-based tissues. Collagen—the most abundant protein in the human body—forms the framework for connective tissue, skin, and blood vessels. Keratin gives hair and nails their structure. Actin and myosin enable muscle contractions. Without a continuous supply of protein, your body cannot maintain, repair, or build these structures.

Enzymatic and regulatory functions

Enzymes – the catalysts for virtually all biochemical reactions in your body – are proteins. Digestive enzymes like pepsin and trypsin break down food proteins into absorbable amino acids. Metabolic enzymes regulate energy production from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. Without sufficient protein building blocks, your body cannot produce enough enzymes, which slows down metabolic processes and impairs the efficiency of your overall metabolism.

Hormones—chemical messengers that regulate virtually every aspect of your physiology—are also frequently proteins or synthesized from amino acids. Insulin, which regulates blood sugar, is a protein. Growth hormone, crucial for regeneration and cell growth, is a protein. Thyroid hormones, which control your metabolism, are made from the amino acid tyrosine. Serotonin and dopamine—neurotransmitters that influence mood and motivation—are synthesized from tryptophan and tyrosine, respectively.

Immune function

Your immune system relies heavily on protein. Antibodies – the proteins that recognize and mark pathogens – must be constantly produced. Immune cells like T lymphocytes and macrophages need protein to multiply and function. Studies show that protein deficiency weakens the immune response and increases susceptibility to infections. Protein requirements rise particularly during periods of increased physical stress or illness to optimally support the immune system.

The benefits of a protein-rich diet

The scientific literature on the benefits of increased protein intake is extensive and compelling. From improved body composition and metabolic health to satiety and weight management – ​​the effects are diverse and well-documented.

Muscle building and muscle maintenance

The most well-known benefit of a protein-rich diet is its support for muscle growth and maintenance. After a workout, your body is in a catabolic state – muscle fibers have been stressed and microscopically damaged. Protein provides the amino acids needed for repair and the building of new muscle fibers. Without sufficient protein, your body cannot convert the training stimuli into muscle growth. Research shows that a protein intake of 1.6 to 2.2 grams per kilogram of body weight is optimal for muscle protein synthesis in active individuals.

Maintaining muscle mass is equally important – especially during periods of calorie deficit or with increasing age. From the age of 30, a gradual loss of muscle mass (sarcopenia) begins, which, without countermeasures, accelerates to 3 to 8 percent per decade. A protein-rich diet combined with strength training is the most effective strategy to counteract this age-related decline and maintain strength, mobility, and independence well into old age.

Weight management and satiety

Protein is the most satiating macronutrient—an effect known as the 'Protein Leverage Hypothesis'. Your body has an inherent need for protein, and as long as this need isn't met, it will continue to signal hunger. People who eat a low-protein diet tend to consume more calories overall to meet their protein requirements—often in the form of excess carbohydrates and fats. A high-protein diet breaks this cycle: You feel full faster, stay full longer, and consume fewer calories overall, without consciously counting calories.

The thermic effect of protein enhances its weight-regulating effect. Approximately 20 to 30 percent of the calories from protein are used for its digestion, absorption, and processing – compared to only 5 to 10 percent for carbohydrates and 0 to 3 percent for fat. This means that of 100 calories from protein, your body effectively only has about 70 to 80 calories available. A high-protein diet therefore increases your calorie expenditure, even if your total calorie intake remains the same.

Metabolic health

Higher protein intake stabilizes blood sugar and improves insulin sensitivity. Protein slows gastric emptying and carbohydrate absorption, thus mitigating post-meal blood sugar spikes. Simultaneously, protein stimulates the release of glucagon—a hormone that counteracts insulin-induced fat storage. Therefore, a protein-prioritized diet can be a valuable therapeutic strategy for individuals with insulin resistance, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes.

The effects on body composition extend beyond mere weight loss. Studies show that, with the same calorie restriction, individuals with higher protein intake lose more fat and less muscle mass than comparison groups with lower protein intake. The result is improved body composition—less body fat with maintained or even increased muscle mass—and a higher basal metabolic rate in the long term.

How much protein do you really need?

The question of the optimal amount of protein is one of the most frequently discussed in nutritional science. The answer is not uniform, but depends on a multitude of individual factors: activity level, training goals, age, body composition, health status, and even genetics all play a role.

The minimum recommendation – and why it is often not enough

The officially recommended daily allowance (RDA) of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight was established in the 1940s and is based on the minimum needed to prevent nitrogen deficiency in sedentary adults. This recommendation was never intended as optimal for health and performance, but rather as a lower limit to avoid deficiencies. For the majority of people—especially active, exercising, or older individuals—this value is insufficient.

Modern research, summarized in meta-analyses and position papers by sports medicine specialists and nutritionists, recommends significantly higher intake levels. For the general adult population, at least 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight is considered a sensible starting point. For physically active individuals who exercise regularly, the recommendation increases to 1.4 to 2.0 grams. Strength athletes and bodybuilders aiming to maximize muscle growth benefit from 1.6 to 2.2 grams or more.

Special situations with increased need

Certain life situations and goals require a more nuanced approach. During a calorie-deficit diet, protein requirements increase to minimize muscle loss – values ​​of 2.0 to 2.4 grams per kilogram of body weight, or even higher, are appropriate here. The greater the calorie deficit, the more important a high protein intake becomes to protect body composition.

Older adults aged 65 and over have an increased protein requirement because the efficiency of protein utilization (anabolic resistance) decreases with age. Recommendations for this age group range from 1.2 to 1.5 grams per kilogram of body weight – some experts advocate even higher values. Protein in combination with resistance training is the most effective strategy against age-related sarcopenia and the associated loss of strength, mobility, and quality of life.

Protein requirements also increase during pregnancy and breastfeeding to support the child's growth and milk production. Similarly, in cases of injury, after surgery, or during illness, the body significantly increases its protein needs for repair and immune processes.

Practical calculation

For practical implementation, a simple approach is recommended: Calculate your protein requirements based on your target weight (not your current weight if you want to lose a significant amount of weight) and your activity level. For someone with a target weight of 75 kilograms who regularly does strength training, this would result in: 75 kg × 1.8 g = 135 grams of protein per day. Divided into three to four meals, this means approximately 35 to 45 grams of protein per meal – a substantial amount that requires conscious planning.

The best protein sources – quality and bioavailability

Not all protein sources are created equal. The quality of a protein is determined by its amino acid composition, digestibility, and bioavailability. Understanding these factors will help you optimize your protein intake and choose the best possible sources for your individual needs.

Complete vs. incomplete proteins

Complete proteins contain all nine essential amino acids in sufficient amounts. Animal protein sources—meat, fish, eggs, dairy products—are typically complete proteins with high bioavailability. Plant protein sources are often incomplete, meaning they lack one or more essential amino acids in optimal amounts. This doesn't mean plant proteins are inferior—a complete amino acid profile can be achieved by cleverly combining different plant sources.

Animal protein sources

Chicken breast is a classic lean protein source: about 31 grams of protein per 100 grams with only 3.6 grams of fat. Beef offers not only high-quality protein but also iron, zinc, and B vitamins – about 26 grams of protein per 100 grams. Fish such as salmon, tuna, or cod provide 20 to 25 grams of protein per 100 grams, and fattier varieties also contain valuable omega-3 fatty acids. Eggs are an excellent all-around protein source with about 13 grams of protein per 100 grams (two large eggs) and a nearly perfect amino acid profile.

Dairy products deserve special mention. Low-fat quark, with approximately 12 grams of protein per 100 grams, is one of the most concentrated and cost-effective protein sources available. Greek yogurt offers similar values. Cheese—depending on the variety—contains 20 to 35 grams of protein per 100 grams, though often with a high fat content. Whey protein from milk is the fastest-absorbed protein and is particularly rich in leucine—the amino acid that most strongly stimulates muscle protein synthesis.

Plant-based protein sources

Adequate protein intake is possible for vegetarians and vegans, but requires more planning. Legumes—lentils, chickpeas, black beans—provide 8 to 9 grams of protein per 100 grams (cooked), but are low in the amino acid methionine. Tofu and tempeh made from soy offer 8 to 20 grams of protein per 100 grams and are one of the few complete plant-based protein sources. Seitan, made from wheat gluten, contains an impressive 25 grams of protein per 100 grams, but is low in lysine.

The solution for a plant-based diet lies in combination: Legumes plus grains (e.g., rice and beans) complement each other to provide a complete amino acid profile. This combination doesn't have to be in the same meal – as long as you consume different plant-based protein sources throughout the day, your body will receive all the essential amino acids.

Protein powders and supplements

Protein powders can be a convenient way to reach protein goals, especially for people with high needs or limited time. Whey protein is considered the gold standard for rapid absorption and high leucine content. Casein is digested more slowly and is suitable for a longer-term protein supply, such as before bed. Plant-based protein powders made from peas, rice, or hemp are alternatives for people who avoid dairy. Remember: Supplements complement a good diet but do not replace it—whole foods provide not only protein but also vitamins, minerals, and phytochemicals.

Understanding amino acids – The building blocks in detail

To truly optimize your protein intake, it's worth taking a closer look at the individual amino acids and their specific functions. Not all amino acids are equally important, and certain situations can increase the need for specific amino acids.

The essential amino acids

Leucine is perhaps the most important amino acid for muscle growth. It directly activates the mTOR signaling pathway, which initiates muscle protein synthesis. Research shows that a meal should contain about 2.5 to 3 grams of leucine to maximally stimulate protein synthesis—this threshold is called the 'leucine threshold'. Animal proteins, especially whey protein, are rich in leucine; plant-based sources typically contain less, which is why larger portions may be necessary.

Isoleucine and valine – known together with leucine as branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) – support muscle protein synthesis and can reduce fatigue during exercise. Lysine is essential for collagen synthesis and calcium absorption. Methionine serves as a precursor to the sulfur-containing amino acid cysteine ​​and is important for detoxification processes. Phenylalanine is a precursor to tyrosine and thus indirectly to neurotransmitters such as dopamine and norepinephrine. Tryptophan is the precursor to serotonin and melatonin – important for mood and sleep. Threonine supports immune function and is a component of mucins, which protect mucous membranes. Histidine is a precursor to histamine and important for wound healing.

Conditionally essential amino acids

Some amino acids are considered conditionally essential – the body can synthesize them, but under certain circumstances, its own production is insufficient. Glutamine is the most abundant amino acid in the blood and is important for gut health and immune function. During periods of stress, intense training, or illness, the body's need for glutamine can exceed its own synthesis. Arginine is a precursor to nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels and improves blood flow. Glycine is important for collagen synthesis and has calming properties.

Monitor the amino acid profile

For people who want to optimize their diet or identify potential deficiencies, an amino acid test can be insightful. Such a test measures the concentrations of various amino acids in the blood and can reveal imbalances or deficiencies. This is particularly relevant for vegetarians and vegans who may be deficient in certain amino acids, for athletes with high requirements, for older people with altered protein utilization, or for people with digestive problems that could impair protein absorption.

The DoctorBox amino acid test allows you to conveniently check your individual amino acid profile from home. Such a test can help you understand whether your current diet provides all essential amino acids in sufficient quantities or whether adjustments would be beneficial. Especially if you are already following a high-protein diet but are experiencing symptoms such as delayed recovery, fatigue, or stagnant muscle growth, a look at your amino acid profile can provide valuable insights.

Protein Timing – When You Should Eat

The question of optimal protein timing has led to endless debates in the fitness and nutrition world. While some consider the 'anabolic window' after training sacrosanct, science paints a more nuanced picture. Timing is relevant, but less critical than the total amount of protein and its distribution throughout the day.

The anabolic window – myth or reality?

The idea behind the anabolic window is that protein must be consumed immediately after training to maximize muscle growth. The reality is more nuanced: there is indeed an increased sensitivity to protein intake post-workout, but this 'window' is wider than often assumed—several hours, not 30 minutes. If you've had a protein-rich meal before training, the amino acids will still be available during and after your workout, making the immediate post-workout shake less critical. However, if you train on an empty stomach or several hours after your last meal, rapid protein intake after training becomes more important.

Distribution throughout the day

More important than precise post-workout timing is the even distribution of protein intake throughout the day. Research shows that several protein-rich meals (typically three to four), each containing 25 to 40 grams of protein, stimulate muscle protein synthesis more effectively than one large protein meal per day. This is due to the so-called 'muscle full' hypothesis: Muscle protein synthesis is elevated by a meal for approximately three to five hours, after which it returns to baseline levels, regardless of how much protein remains in the system. To stimulate synthesis multiple times a day, you need to repeatedly exceed the leucine threshold of approximately 2.5 to 3 grams per meal.

A typical distribution pattern could look like this: breakfast with 30-40 grams of protein (e.g., eggs with quark), lunch with 35-45 grams (e.g., chicken with vegetables), dinner with 35-45 grams (e.g., fish with salad), and possibly a protein-rich snack (e.g., Greek yogurt). The exact figures vary depending on individual needs.

Protein before sleep

One often overlooked time is the evening. During sleep, your body undergoes important regeneration processes that require protein. A protein-rich meal or snack before bed—ideally with slow-digesting protein like casein—can support nighttime muscle protein synthesis. Studies show that 30 to 40 grams of casein before bed can improve regeneration without compromising sleep quality or increasing fat storage.

Synchronize protein and training

For optimal results, you should roughly synchronize your protein intake with your training. This doesn't mean you have to drink a shake immediately after every workout, but rather that you ensure you're getting enough protein in the hours surrounding your training (before and after). A practical rule of thumb: Have a protein-rich meal within three hours before and three hours after your workout. Within this timeframe, it's less important whether you eat directly before or directly after your workout.

High-protein for various diets

A protein-prioritized diet is compatible with virtually any dietary philosophy – from omnivorous to vegetarian and vegan, to low-carb or keto. The implementation varies, but the basic principle remains: prioritize protein and build meals around protein-rich foods.

High-protein omnivore

For omnivores, implementation is easiest. The variety of animal and plant-based protein sources allows for flexible meal planning. A typical day might look like this: breakfast with scrambled eggs and smoked salmon, lunch with chicken breast on a salad, dinner with beef tenderloin and vegetables, and Greek yogurt as a snack in between. The challenge lies less in the availability of options than in conscious prioritization – it's easy to fall back into old habits and structure meals around carbohydrates rather than protein.

High-protein vegetarian

Vegetarians can relatively easily achieve high protein intake with eggs and dairy products. Low-fat quark, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, and eggs are cornerstones of a vegetarian high-protein diet. Legumes, tofu, and tempeh round out the options. A typical day: breakfast with oatmeal, protein powder, and nuts; lunch with lentil soup and feta; dinner with tofu stir-fry and quinoa; snacks of cottage cheese or hard-boiled eggs.

The challenge for vegetarians lies in the higher calorie density of many protein-rich plant-based foods. While 100 grams of chicken breast provides about 31 grams of protein with only 165 calories, the same amount of protein from lentils contains significantly more calories and carbohydrates. For vegetarians who want to lose weight, this can make it difficult to maintain a balanced macronutrient intake.

High-protein vegan

A vegan high-protein diet is possible, but requires meticulous planning. Without animal products, the importance of soy protein (tofu, tempeh, edamame), seitan, legumes, and plant-based protein powders increases. Combining different protein sources becomes critical to obtaining all essential amino acids in sufficient quantities. A typical day: breakfast with tofu scramble and whole-wheat bread; lunch with chickpea curry and rice; dinner with seitan strips and vegetables; snacks of edamame or a vegan protein shake.

The amino acids leucine and lysine, which are often underrepresented in plant-based sources, deserve special attention. Vegan athletes may benefit from higher total protein intake (approximately 10-20 percent more than omnivores) to compensate for the lower bioavailability and suboptimal amino acid profile. An amino acid test can help identify potential deficiencies.

High protein low carb or keto

The combination of high-protein with low-carb or keto diets is natural, as both approaches inherently involve a reduction in carbohydrates in favor of other macronutrients. Caution is advised with strict ketosis: too much protein can disrupt ketosis through gluconeogenesis (the conversion of amino acids into glucose). However, for most people not aiming for therapeutic ketosis, this isn't a practical problem – a moderate keto diet with high protein intake is well-tolerated and, for many, more sustainable than a fat-dominant, low-protein keto approach.

Common Concerns and Myths

Numerous myths and concerns surround the topic of protein – from supposed kidney damage and bone loss to the worry that excess protein is automatically converted into fat. A look at the scientific evidence helps to separate fact from fiction.

Does high protein intake harm the kidneys?

This is one of the most persistent myths. It originates from the observation that people with pre-existing kidney disease should restrict their protein intake to protect their remaining kidney function. From this, it was mistakenly concluded that high protein intake causes kidney disease. However, the evidence shows the opposite: In people with healthy kidneys, there is no evidence that even very high protein intake (over 2 g per kg of body weight over many years) impairs kidney function.

Long-term studies of strength athletes and bodybuilders who routinely consume 2 to 3 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight show no increased rates of kidney disease. The kidneys are remarkably adaptable and simply increase their filtration capacity with higher protein intake—much like muscles get stronger with regular exercise. However, if you already suffer from kidney disease, you should discuss your protein intake with your doctor.

Does protein leach calcium from bones?

The theory states that protein has an acidifying effect, and the body mobilizes calcium from the bones to balance the acid-base levels. Earlier studies seemed to support this, as higher protein intake led to increased calcium levels in the urine. However, more recent, better-controlled studies show that the increased calcium excretion is compensated for by improved calcium absorption from the intestines. The net calcium balance remains neutral or even improves.

Protein is indeed essential for bone health: Approximately 50 percent of bone volume consists of protein (mainly collagen). Epidemiological studies show that higher protein intake is associated with better bone mineral density and a lower fracture risk—provided calcium intake is also sufficient. The combination of protein and calcium appears to have a synergistic effect on bone health.

Does excess protein become fat?

Biochemically, the body can convert excess amino acids into fatty acids through complex metabolic pathways. In practice, however, this process is so inefficient that it is hardly relevant under normal nutritional conditions. The conversion of protein into fat (de novo lipogenesis from amino acids) requires considerable energy and is the body's last resort when all other utilization pathways have been exhausted.

Overeating studies, in which participants intentionally consumed excessive calories from protein, showed that weight gain was less than with equivalent calorie surpluses from carbohydrates or fat. The high thermic effect of protein (20-30 percent of calories are used for digestion) partially explains this phenomenon. This doesn't mean you can eat unlimited amounts of protein without gaining weight, but it does mean that protein is the most forgiving macronutrient when consumed in excess.

Practical implementation – your path to a high-protein diet

Knowing the theory is one thing – putting it into practice in everyday life is another. Here are concrete strategies to successfully increase your protein intake and establish a sustainable protein-prioritized diet.

Step 1: Inventory

Before making any changes, it's helpful to know where you stand. Track your normal diet for a week using an app like MyFitnessPal or Cronometer. Pay particular attention to your average daily protein intake and how it's distributed across meals. Many people are surprised by how little protein they actually consume—often less than 60 grams per day—even though they believe they eat a 'protein-rich' diet.

Step 2: Define the goal

Based on your body weight, goals, and activity level, define a specific daily protein goal. A moderate goal is recommended to start with, which you can gradually increase. If you currently eat 70 grams of protein per day and your goal is 140 grams, don't plan to reach the full amount tomorrow. First, increase to 90-100 grams, get used to it, and then increase further.

Step 3: Restructure meals

The key is to plan each meal around a substantial protein source. Instead of asking, 'What am I eating today?', ask, 'What protein am I eating today?' Breakfast is often the biggest area for improvement: swap cereal or toast for eggs, quark, Greek yogurt, or a protein shake. Increasing your protein intake at breakfast from just 10 to 30 grams can make all the difference.

Lunch and dinner are typically easier to adjust – increase the portion size of the protein component and reduce side dishes if necessary. Instead of 100 grams of chicken with 200 grams of rice, make 180 grams of chicken with 120 grams of rice. The calorie count remains similar, but the protein content increases significantly.

Step 4: Strategic Snacks

Protein-rich snacks can help fill gaps in your diet. Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, hard-boiled eggs, beef jerky, protein bars, or a protein shake are convenient options for when you're on the go. Avoid classic snacks like chips, cookies, or fruit alone—they provide very little protein and can trigger cravings.

Step 5: Preparation is everything

Meal prep—cooking meals in advance—is a powerful tool for a successful high-protein diet. Cook larger quantities of protein (grilled chicken, hard-boiled eggs, marinated tofu) on the weekend and store it in the refrigerator. This way, you always have a protein source readily available and don't have to resort to suboptimal options when hunger strikes. A well-stocked refrigerator with prepared protein sources is your best insurance against unhealthy impulse buys.
